synopsis: The corpus rejects a single simulation hardware specification: logic and object-list tests suit commodity CPUs or cloud containers, sensor rendering suits GPU workers, soil simulation suits dedicated GPU/HPC workers, and HIL needs a local deterministic real-time system [f8839, f16220]. Radar figures illustrate workload-dependent performance: a vendor CPU solver took 14 hours for a 12-second scenario, a vendor GPU solver reported about 12 ms per frame, and independent RadaRays measurements ranged from 7.8–18.8 ms per image on an RTX 2070 Super, only for the tested radar, model and scene [f4931, f12961, f4936]. CARLA UE5 requires at least an RTX 3000-series GPU with 16 GB VRAM and 130 GB disk, while Chrono CRM requires an NVIDIA GPU and reportedly runs 50–200 times slower than real time; consumer hardware can also struggle with fields containing thousands of vegetation assets [f8469, f8851, f15989, f3895]. For HIL, timing matters more than throughput: missing a required sensor-message deadline of 50 milliseconds can produce a false test result [f16187, f16179]. The cloud-budget example buys about 29,000 GPU-hours for USD 54,490 using ten single-GPU instances continuously for 122 days, but actual geometry, sensors and achieved real-time factors must be benchmarked before infrastructure commitments [f16226, f16190, f10832]. Remaining sizing gaps include insufficient mostly on-road neural-rendering evidence and unestablished data rates, storage sizes and ruggedized logger requirements for continuous raw recording on working machines [f4948, f5801].
